transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-03
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sanjay (AE), Maya (SE), Luis (Solutions) - Redwood; Alicia (CTO), Ben (Platform), Priya (ML Infra), Tom (Security) - EquityLabs

Summary: Short discovery focused on dedicated GPU tenancy, tenant isolation patterns, burst/fallback to hosted, prewarm/hot-pool strategies, and compliance (data residency + KMS). Customer is evaluating private vs dedicated; primary ask is predictable latency under market open load spikes and strict isolation between clients.

Topics touched: dedicated capacity sizing, tenancy/isolation models (node-level, pod-level, multi-tenant GPU), prewarm/hot-pool, burst to Redwood hosted, GPU types (A100 vs H100), autoscaling policies, preemption & spot concerns, encryption/KMS and audit trails, canary rollout and fallback, cost modeling, pilot next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sanjay: hey thanks everyone for joining, we, um, appreciate you taking the time. quick round of intros?
[00:06] Alicia: hi im Alicia, CTO at EquityLabs. we're building low-latency inferencing for our trader desk workflows, and our big constraint is spikes during market opens.
[00:13] Ben: ben here, i run platform, we have an eks cluster plus some on-prem gpu racks.
[00:18] Priya: priya, ml infra; worried about kv cache warmup and how model state is preserved across bursts.
[00:23] Tom: tom, security; i'll be focused on sso/kms and audit logs.
[00:27] Sanjay: great, maya from our infra team will cover the deep capacity stuff, maya?
[00:31] Maya: thanks, hi everyone, so i'd like to understand three things: expected concurrency, burst factor, and isolation needs. can you give ballpark numbers?
[00:40] Alicia: baseline is 80 qps across models, and during market open we see 12x spike for 5-8 minutes, so peak ~960 qps. target p99 latency is sub-200ms for short prompts.
[00:52] Ben: note most requests are short; token lengths avg 24 tokens. we also have a few long-form summaries but those are not on the critical path.
[00:58] Maya: okay that helps. are you open to mixing dedicated reserved gpus plus burst to hosted instances?
[01:04] Alicia: yes — we want a reserved pool for baseline plus a fast path to burst. key requirement: no cross-tenant leakage and logs retained for 12 months in EU.
[01:12] Tom: also need KMS integration; customer keys must never leave our vault.
[01:16] Luis: quick clarifying q, when you say tenant do you mean customer-facing tenant or internal teams?
[01:20] Alicia: customer-facing tenants. we have regulatory clients that require physical isolation for some customers.
[01:25] Maya: two patterns we see: single-tenant nodes (physical isolation per customer) or multi-tenant with strict pod/node taints and runtime sandboxing. single-tenant increases cost but simplifies compliance.
[01:36] Priya: for those regulatory clients we prefer single-tenant nodes, yes. for the rest multi-tenant with cgroups + network policies is ok.
[01:44] Maya: good. about burst — our Dedicated product supports hot-pools and prewarmed instances that keep weights in memory. you can configure a reserved pool sized for baseline plus a burst policy that calls hosted endpoints when reserved capacity is exhausted. the fallback can be to a quantized variant or to hosted identical model depending on your latency tolerance.
[02:00] Ben: whats the warmup time you're seeing for an h100 vs a100 if weights need to be loaded?
[02:06] Maya: rough numbers: h100 cold load can be 25–40s depending on weight IO and sequence length; with prewarm/hotpool we can keep KV cache and weights resident so warm starts are sub-1s. a100 similar cold times but slightly slower for large models.
[02:18] Priya: that's helpful - we can't afford 25s cold on open.
[02:21] Maya: exactly which is why prewarm matters; you can also configure a small rolling warm pool that keeps N replicas ready.
[02:28] Alicia: ok, what's the tradeoff on cost? how big should the reserved pool be?
[02:33] Sanjay: we normally recommend sizing reserved for 40-70% of expected peak, combined with an autoscaler and burst policy. we also provide cost models showing per-hour reserved vs per-token hosted costs. i'll share a spreadsheet.
[02:44] Ben: curious about GPU types — should we go H100 for the reserved nodes? we have on-prem H100s for some workloads.
[02:50] Maya: h100 gives better throughput for some transformer ops, but quantization and kernel selection matter. for predictable latency a smaller pool of h100s with prewarm gives better tail latency. if you already have on-prem h100s we can integrate them with Private or Dedicated depending on control plane access.
[03:05] Priya: integration meaning what? can we keep our keys in KMS and have Redwood never see plaintext?
[03:10] Maya: yes — for Private deployments we support customer-managed control plane and HSM/KMS integrations so model data and keys remain in your VPC. for Dedicated (Redwood-managed), we offer envelope encryption with customer KMS for some enterprise contracts; we'll include the exact diagram in the security docs.
[03:24] Tom: and audit logs? retention and which fields are stored?
[03:27] Luis: we export token-level and request-level traces. for PII we can redact payloads; audit logs include model version, timestamp, request id, route, and user identity. retention configurable up to 2 years for an add-on.
[03:41] Alicia: important — we need EU data residency and 12-month retention.
[03:45] Maya: we have EU-hosted regions and you can lock a Dedicated pool to region. we'll confirm the region locations in the docs.
[03:52] Ben: what about tenancy isolation within the same GPU across containers? can we pin vGPU or enforce hardware-level isolation?
[03:58] Maya: we don't do vGPU in the traditional partitioning sense for some of the large models; isolation is achieved via node-level scheduling and kernel sandboxing. for strict regulatory tenants we recommend physical isolation nodes. we can support PCIe passthrough style setups in some Private deployments if needed.
[04:12] Priya: ok good. on preemption and spot — do you ever preempt in Dedicated?
[04:16] Maya: Dedicated reserved capacity is non-preemptible. burst to hosted might use a mix of spot/backfill in non-critical pools but we can configure fallback to quantized model in region or throttle.
[04:25] Ben: latency SLOs on hosted fallback — how much variance?
[04:28] Luis: typically fallback to hosted identical model adds 10–30ms network + possible queuing; if fallback uses a quantized variant expect 30–120ms variance depending on model size and batch.
[04:40] Alicia: we need a plan for A/B canary: if we do a rollout and the hosted fallback is used during spikes, how do we preserve user experience?
[04:48] Maya: we support traffic splitting at route level, canary thresholds, and automatic rollback. plus real-time quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[04:57] Priya: curious about KV cache across replicas — if a request hits a hot replica vs a cold one, do you have graceful degradation?
[05:04] Maya: yes we try to route by cache affinity for high QPS workloads. we also maintain per-tenant warm pools so most requests hit warm replicas. when not available, we spill to fallback and populate cache. there will be brief p50/p90 differences but we minimize p99 tail with warm pools.
[05:18] Tom: from security side, can we get a SOC2 report and a network diagram?
[05:22] Sanjay: absolutely, we'll send SOC2 + ISO summary and network & keyflow diagrams.
[05:26] Alicia: thinking of an initial pilot: 4-week reserved pool for EU region with single-tenant nodes for 3 regulated customers and a multi-tenant pool for the rest. then evaluate scaling to US region.
[05:36] Sanjay: that sounds reasonable. our typical pilot includes a baseline reserved commit and daily/weekly benchmarks to tune batch sizes and prewarm counts.
[05:44] Ben: benchmarks — can you run against our on-prem H100s or do you need us to ship logs?
[05:49] Maya: we can run two kinds: in-situ on your hardware (Private pilot) or we run identical workloads in our hosted/dedicated environment. for on-prem we'll need a short connector and access to a staging cluster.
[05:59] Priya: estimated time to spin up a reserved pool?
[06:02] Maya: in our experience, provisioning reserved nodes into a Dedicated pool takes 48–72 hours once terms and region are confirmed; hot-pools and prewarm config are operationally quick. for Private on-prem deploys, plan for 2–4 weeks depending on networking and KMS integration.
[06:15] Alicia: pricing ask — committed hours vs token pricing, what do you typically offer for a 4-week pilot?
[06:21] Sanjay: pilot pricing is usually a small reserved commit + usage caps; we'll provide 3 tier examples in the spreadsheet — low reserved, medium reserved with larger hot-pool, and higher reserved sized for 70% peak.
[06:33] Ben: any contract minimums?
[06:35] Sanjay: for Dedicated we do monthly minimums for reserved pools; exact numbers in the proposal. pilots can be structured as time-boxed evals with credits.
[06:44] Priya: technical nit — how do you handle GPU kernel selection and quantized kernels? if we use 4-bit quantized models will we see large perf differences?
[06:53] Maya: yes quantization can change throughput and latency tradeoffs. our runtime picks kernels based on model arch and sequence length; for many workloads 4-bit gives 2-3x token throughput but you'll want to validate quality. we'll include our quantization matrix in the tech notes.
[07:06] Alicia: last — who will be our point people?
[07:09] Sanjay: primary AE is me, se lead is maya; luis will coordinate onboarding and pricing. who from your side will own the pilot?
[07:15] Alicia: i'll own the pilot, ben and priya will be day-to-day. tom handles approvals.
[07:19] Sanjay: perfect. recap and next steps: we'll send pricing, security docs, and propose pilot scope; maya will prepare concurrency charts and a sample warm-pool config; schedule a 2-hour benchmark windows week of Dec 13.
[07:32] Ben: works for me.
[07:33] Priya: ok.
[07:34] Tom: sounds good.
[07:36] Sanjay: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc bundle and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[07:41] Alicia: thanks all.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-labelled speaker in a couple of lines, a few words misheard (e.g., "prewarm" transcribed as "pre-worm" in one place), some punctuation dropped.
